title: Pathophysiology: Infection—From Exposure and Colonization to Sepsis
html:
Infection develops when a microorganism reaches a susceptible host, enters or bypasses defenses, multiplies, and produces tissue damage or a harmful host response. Exposure does not always lead to infection, and the presence of an organism does not automatically mean disease. The RN connects the organism, route, site, host response, and time course to recognize both transmission risk and clinical deterioration.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish contamination, colonization, local infection, systemic infection, bacteremia, and sepsis.
  • Explain how portals of entry, microbial virulence, inoculum, and host defenses shape disease.
  • Compare common patterns of bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infection without diagnosing from one cue.
  • Use the chain of infection to select prevention measures.
  • Interpret cultures and inflammatory findings in context.
  • Recognize organ dysfunction that may signal sepsis and requires urgent escalation.
  • Evaluate response to source control, antimicrobial therapy, and supportive care.

Presence of a microorganism is not always infection

Contamination means an organism is introduced into a specimen, surface, or site without representing true growth in the client. Colonization means organisms live on or in the body without causing symptoms or tissue invasion; a colonized person may still transmit them. Infection involves invasion and multiplication with tissue response, symptoms, or both. Distinguishing these states prevents both missed disease and unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.

Do not treat a culture result in isolation
Interpret the specimen source, collection quality, organism, quantity, symptoms, devices, host risks, prior antimicrobials, and timing. A positive culture may reflect infection, colonization, or contamination; a negative culture does not exclude infection after antibiotics or with difficult-to-grow organisms.

The chain of infection identifies prevention points

Transmission requires an infectious agent, a reservoir, a portal of exit, a mode of transmission, a portal of entry, and a susceptible host. Breaking any link can reduce spread. Hand hygiene, source control, respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning, safe injection practices, device care, personal protective equipment, vaccination, and appropriate isolation precautions interrupt different links.

Standard Precautions apply to every client based on anticipated exposure. Transmission-Based Precautions add contact, droplet, or airborne measures for organisms or syndromes with relevant routes. Route is not determined only by the body system affected, so the RN follows current organism-specific guidance and organizational policy.

Pathogenesis depends on organism and host

Pathogenicity describes the ability to cause disease, while virulence reflects the degree of harm. Adhesion factors help organisms attach; capsules and biofilms can resist clearance; enzymes may promote invasion; toxins can directly alter cells or trigger inflammation. A larger inoculum or direct entry through an invasive device can overwhelm defenses that would otherwise contain exposure.

Host susceptibility changes with age, nutrition, skin and mucosal integrity, perfusion, chronic illness, vaccination, pregnancy, immune function, medication exposure, surgery, and devices. The same organism may cause asymptomatic colonization in one person and invasive disease in another.

Microbial groups use different strategies

Bacteria can multiply extracellularly or within cells and may injure tissue through invasion, toxins, and the host inflammatory response. Viruses require host cells for replication and can injure cells directly or through immune-mediated damage. Fungi range from superficial disease to opportunistic invasive infection. Parasites include protozoa and helminths with diverse life cycles and exposure routes.

Symptoms, white blood cell patterns, drainage color, or fever alone cannot reliably identify the group. Diagnostic reasoning integrates epidemiology, exposure, site, host status, imaging, microscopy, antigen or molecular tests, serology, and properly collected cultures.

Local infection can extend or disseminate

A local infection may cause pain, warmth or color change, swelling, purulent drainage, impaired function, or organ-specific symptoms. Lymphatic spread may cause tender nodes or streaking. Organisms or their products can enter blood and reach distant sites. Bacteremia means viable bacteria are present in blood; it can be transient, persistent, or associated with severe illness. Bacteremia is not synonymous with sepsis.

Systemic findings may include fever or hypothermia, chills, malaise, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered glucose, and leukocyte changes. Older adults, newborns, and immunocompromised clients may show muted or atypical responses such as confusion, functional decline, poor feeding, or hypothermia.

Biofilms and devices change infection risk

Microorganisms can attach to catheters, prosthetic material, wounds, or damaged tissue and form a biofilm: an organized community embedded in a protective matrix. Biofilms reduce penetration by immune defenses and some antimicrobial agents and can seed persistent or recurrent infection. Preventing unnecessary device use, using aseptic insertion and access, maintaining closed systems, and removing devices as soon as no longer indicated reduce risk.

Specimens must answer the clinical question

Collect cultures from the suspected site using the correct container, technique, volume, and timing. When ordered and feasible, obtain cultures before the first antimicrobial dose, but never delay emergency stabilization or time-critical therapy solely to collect a specimen. Label at the bedside and communicate the exact source; "wound culture" without a location is insufficient.

Culture identifies growth under laboratory conditions. Susceptibility testing estimates which antimicrobials inhibit the organism. Molecular tests detect genetic material and may remain positive when viable organisms are absent. Serology reflects an antibody response and depends strongly on timing. Every result must be reconciled with the clinical picture.

Antimicrobial resistance changes treatment—not basic precautions

Resistance allows a microorganism to survive exposure to an antimicrobial that would normally inhibit it. Selection pressure from unnecessary, overly broad, or incomplete therapy promotes survival of resistant populations. Antimicrobial stewardship uses the right agent, dose, route, and duration and narrows or stops therapy when evidence supports doing so.

The RN obtains ordered specimens, checks allergy and organ-function information, administers time-critical therapy, monitors adverse effects, and supports reassessment. Never save, share, or independently restart leftover antibiotics. Improvement does not authorize changing the prescribed course without the treating team.

Sepsis is infection with a dangerous systemic response

Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection that can cause tissue damage, organ dysfunction, and death. It is not defined by fever alone, and a client can be septic without fever or a positive blood culture. Concerning cues include new hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypoxemia, oliguria, mottling, delayed capillary refill, rising lactate, thrombocytopenia, or worsening organ tests.

Prioritize organ dysfunction over the temperature number
A client with suspected infection plus new confusion, respiratory distress, low blood pressure, or falling urine output needs immediate assessment and the organization's sepsis or emergency pathway. Do not wait for every laboratory result or for a high fever.

Source control and support are both essential

Antimicrobials may not succeed if infected material or a contaminated device remains. Source control can include drainage, debridement, relief of obstruction, removal of an infected device, or surgery. Nursing priorities include airway and oxygenation support, perfusion assessment, ordered fluids and medications, timely specimens, glucose and output monitoring, device review, and frequent evaluation for benefit or harm.

Evaluate trends, not isolated improvements

Useful outcomes include improving mental status, work of breathing, blood pressure, perfusion, urine output, pain, function, temperature trend, and laboratory markers. A lower temperature after an antipyretic does not prove infection control. Persistent hypotension, increasing oxygen need, declining urine output, new rash, worsening pain, or organ dysfunction requires escalation even if one laboratory value improves.

Translate infection into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize: Identify exposure, site, onset, symptoms, device or procedure risks, immune status, vital-sign trends, perfusion, and organ function.
  2. Analyze: Decide whether findings fit contamination, colonization, local infection, systemic spread, medication effect, or another cause.
  3. Prioritize: Airway compromise, shock, respiratory distress, altered mental status, oliguria, and rapidly progressing tissue injury outrank routine teaching.
  4. Generate: Plan isolation, specimen collection, source control, prescribed therapy, supportive care, communication, and reassessment.
  5. Act: Apply Standard and indicated Transmission-Based Precautions, stabilize the client, follow time-critical pathways, and document the trend.
  6. Evaluate: Reassess symptoms, perfusion, organ function, cultures, susceptibilities, therapy response, adverse effects, and need for source control.

Clinical example

A client with an indwelling urinary catheter becomes newly confused and tachypneic. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), blood pressure is falling, and urine output has decreased. Cloudy urine alone would be nonspecific, but the acute organ-function and perfusion changes create a high-risk cluster. The RN assesses ABCs and perfusion, activates the appropriate sepsis pathway, obtains ordered specimens without delaying treatment, reviews the catheter's necessity, administers prescribed therapy, and repeatedly evaluates response.
